items.meaning: Like MLE, but also rewards parameters the prior considers plausible; the log-prior becomes a penalty term in the loss. τ^2 (tau squared) is the prior variance: a tighter prior means stronger regularization.
items.used_for: Explains L2 penalties and weight decay (implementations in deep-learning) and L1 sparsity (lasso, classical-ml); add-one smoothing of counts; priors in Bayesian optimization. Book: Only here (regularization in Chapters 9 and 13).

items.name: Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound
items.formula: `I(θ) = E[(∂ ln p(x given θ) ÷ ∂θ)^2] = −E[∂^2 ln p(x given θ) ÷ ∂θ^2]`; matrix form `F = E[∇_θ ln p × (∇_θ ln p)^T]`; Cramér–Rao `Var(θ_hat) ≥ 1 ÷ (n × I(θ))` for unbiased estimators; `KL(p_θ || p_(θ + δ)) ≈ (1 ÷ 2) × δ^T × F × δ`
items.meaning: How much one observation tells you about a parameter: the expected squared slope of the log-likelihood, which equals its expected curvature. More information means a tighter best-possible estimate. The Fisher matrix F also measures how much a small parameter change δ alters the model's output distribution.
items.used_for: Natural-gradient and K-FAC optimizers; TRPO's trust region (rl-alignment); elastic weight consolidation against catastrophic forgetting weights each parameter by its Fisher value (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017); Fisher-weighted model merging; Laplace approximations for uncertainty. Book: Only here.

items.name: Information content (surprisal), bits and nats
items.formula: `I(x) = −log2(P(x))` bits, or `−ln(P(x))` nats; `1 nat = 1 ÷ ln(2) ≈ 1.443 bits`; bits needed to index K equally likely items `log2(K)`
items.meaning: Rarer events carry more information: probability 1/2 is 1 bit, 1/4 is 2 bits, 1/1024 is 10 bits. Natural logs give nats, the unit most training losses use.
items.used_for: The per-token training loss is the surprisal of the correct token in nats; bits-per-byte and bits-per-character reporting of language-model quality; a 100,000-token vocabulary needs log2(100,000) ≈ 16.6, so 17 bits per token ID; compression and watermark-detection scores. Book: Chapter 6 (Cross-entropy); Appendix B (Bits of surprise).

items.name: Entropy
items.formula: `H(X) = −sum over x of P(x) × log P(x) = E[−log P(X)]`; binary `H(p) = −p × log(p) − (1 − p) × log(1 − p)`; `0 ≤ H(X) ≤ log(K)`, the maximum reached by the uniform distribution; Gaussian (differential entropy) `(1 ÷ 2) × ln(2 × π × e × σ^2)`
items.meaning: The average surprise of a distribution: how unpredictable it is. A fair coin has 1 bit (ln 2 ≈ 0.693 nats); a certain outcome has 0. It is the lowest average loss any model can reach on data from that distribution.
items.used_for: Entropy of the next-token distribution as an uncertainty signal and in decoding methods (llm); entropy bonuses and watching for entropy collapse during RL fine-tuning (rl-alignment); semantic entropy over clusters of sampled answers to detect confabulations (Farquhar et al., Nature 2024); decision-tree information gain (classical-ml); the maximum-entropy derivation of softmax. Book: Chapter 6 (Entropy definition).

items.name: Cross-entropy
items.formula: `H(p, q) = −sum over x of p(x) × log q(x)`; `H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p || q) ≥ H(p)`; one observed outcome y (p one-hot): `H = −log q(y)`
items.meaning: The average surprise when reality follows p but you predict with q. It can never beat the true entropy H(p); the excess is the KL divergence. With a one-hot target it is minus the log probability of the correct answer (the training-loss form, including label smoothing, is in deep-learning).
items.used_for: The standard loss for classification and next-token prediction; knowledge distillation with soft teacher targets (llm); contrastive objectives (generative-classical). Book: Chapter 6 (Cross-entropy: how surprised was the model?); Appendix B.

items.name: Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence
items.formula: `KL(p || q) = sum over x of p(x) × log(p(x) ÷ q(x)) = H(p, q) − H(p)`; `KL ≥ 0`, zero only when p = q; not symmetric: `KL(p || q) ≠ KL(q || p)`; Gaussians `KL(N(μ_1, σ_1^2) || N(μ_2, σ_2^2)) = ln(σ_2 ÷ σ_1) + (σ_1^2 + (μ_1 − μ_2)^2) ÷ (2 × σ_2^2) − 1 ÷ 2`
items.meaning: The extra surprise from believing q when the truth is p. Minimizing forward KL(p || q) makes q cover everything p does (mass-covering); minimizing reverse KL(q || p) makes q lock onto one mode of p (mode-seeking).
items.used_for: The KL penalty that keeps an RLHF- or RL-tuned model close to its reference model, and its sample estimators (rl-alignment); the VAE regularizer (generative-classical); forward- or reverse-KL distillation losses (llm); trust regions in PPO and TRPO; measuring drift between model versions. Book: Chapter 6 (KL divergence definition), Chapter 20 (KL leash).

items.name: Joint entropy, conditional entropy and the entropy chain rule
items.formula: `H(X, Y) = −sum over x, y of P(x, y) × log P(x, y)`; `H(Y given X) = −sum over x, y of P(x, y) × log P(y given x) = H(X, Y) − H(X)`; chain rule `H(X_1, ..., X_n) = sum over t of H(X_t given X_1, ..., X_(t − 1))`; `H(Y given X) ≤ H(Y)`
items.meaning: Conditional entropy is the uncertainty left in Y once X is known; on average, knowing more never increases uncertainty. The chain rule mirrors the chain rule of probability: a sequence's total entropy is the sum of its per-step conditional entropies.
items.used_for: A language model's average per-token loss estimates (from above) the conditional entropy of the next token given its context; information gain in decision trees (classical-ml); measuring how much extra context helps prediction. Book: Only here.

items.name: Mutual information (and the data-processing inequality)
items.formula: `I(X; Y) = H(X) − H(X given Y) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X, Y) = sum over x, y of P(x, y) × log(P(x, y) ÷ (P(x) × P(y))) = KL(P(x, y) || P(x) × P(y))`; data processing: if X → Y → Z form a Markov chain, `I(X; Z) ≤ I(X; Y)`
items.meaning: How much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about the other; zero exactly when they are independent. Processing data can never create new information about its source.
items.used_for: Contrastive objectives such as InfoNCE maximize a lower bound on the mutual information between two views (generative-classical); feature selection (classical-ml); the information-bottleneck view of representations; measuring how much a probe or a watermark reveals. Book: Only here.

items.name: Perplexity (and bits per byte)
items.formula: `perplexity = exp(H)` with entropy or cross-entropy H in nats (`2^H` with H in bits); for a text of N tokens `PPL = exp(−(1 ÷ N) × sum over t of ln q(x_t given x_<t))`; bits per byte `= (total loss in nats) ÷ (ln(2) × number of bytes)`
items.meaning: Exponentiated average surprise: the number of equally likely options the model is effectively choosing among. A fair coin has perplexity 2; a uniform choice among K options has perplexity K. Bits per byte measures the same loss per byte of raw text, so models with different tokenizers can be compared.
items.used_for: The standard intrinsic metric for language models and for tracking pretraining; filtering training data by a reference model's perplexity (llm); detecting machine-generated text. Book: Chapter 6 (Perplexity); Appendix B.

items.name: Jensen–Shannon divergence
items.meaning: A symmetric, always-finite version of KL that compares each distribution with their average m. Its square root is a true distance.
items.used_for: With an optimal discriminator, the original GAN objective equals 2 × JS − 2 × ln(2) (Goodfellow et al. 2014; generative-classical); comparing token or topic distributions between datasets; measuring diversity and agreement among model outputs. Book: Only here.

items.name: f-divergences and total variation distance
items.formula: `D_f(p || q) = sum over x of q(x) × f(p(x) ÷ q(x))` for convex f with f(1) = 0 (KL uses `f(t) = t × ln(t)`); total variation `TV(p, q) = (1 ÷ 2) × sum over x of |p(x) − q(x)|`; Pinsker's inequality `TV(p, q) ≤ sqrt(KL(p || q) ÷ 2)`
items.meaning: A family of ways to measure how different two distributions are; KL, reverse KL, Jensen–Shannon, chi-squared and total variation are all members. Total variation is the largest difference in probability the two distributions can give any event.
items.used_for: Speculative decoding accepts a draft token with overall probability 1 − TV between the draft and target distributions (Leviathan et al. 2023; llm); f-GANs (generative-classical); Pinsker's inequality turns KL bounds into probability bounds in RL and safety analyses; alternative divergences for distillation. Book: Only here.

items.name: Source coding bound (compression equals prediction)
items.formula: average code length `L ≥ H(X)` bits per symbol; an ideal code (arithmetic coding) spends about `−log2 q(x)` bits on symbol x, so a whole text costs about `sum over t of −log2 q(x_t given x_<t)` bits
items.meaning: No lossless code can beat the entropy on average, and a good probability model yields a code that nearly reaches it: each bit of cross-entropy loss is a bit of compressed file size. Better prediction means better compression.
items.used_for: 'Language Modeling Is Compression' (Delétang et al., ICLR 2024) used Chinchilla 70B with arithmetic coding to compress ImageNet patches to 43.4% and LibriSpeech audio to 16.4% of raw size, beating PNG (58.5%) and FLAC (30.3%); bits-per-byte evaluation; the compression view of pretraining loss. Book: Only here.

items.name: Gradient descent update (and the minibatch gradient)
items.formula: `θ_(t+1) = θ_t − η × ∇L(θ_t)`; minibatch estimate `g = (1 ÷ B) × sum over i in the batch of ∇ℓ_i(θ)`, with `E[g] = ∇L(θ)` and variance falling as `1 ÷ B`
items.meaning: Move every parameter a small step against its slope; η (eta) is the learning rate and θ the parameters. In stochastic gradient descent the gradient is estimated from a random batch of B examples (ℓ_i is example i's loss): unbiased but noisy. Momentum, Adam, Muon and learning-rate schedules are in deep-learning.
items.used_for: The core of training every neural network, from a small classifier to a frontier LLM. Book: Chapter 6 (Gradient descent: walking downhill in fog), Chapter 13; Appendix B (Gradient descent step).

items.name: Optimality conditions (stationary points, minima and saddle points)
items.formula: first-order necessary condition `∇f(x*) = 0`; second-order: at a minimum the Hessian `H(x*)` is positive semidefinite, and positive definite is enough for a strict local minimum; saddle point: `∇f = 0` with H having both positive and negative eigenvalues
items.meaning: At the bottom of a valley the slope is zero in every direction and the surface curves upward. A flat point that curves up in some directions and down in others is a saddle; in very high dimensions most flat points are saddles rather than poor local minima.
items.used_for: Explains plateaus and saddle escapes in deep-network training, helped by SGD noise; using the gradient norm to judge convergence; closed-form solutions found by setting the gradient to zero (least squares, MLE). Book: Chapter 6 (Valleys, plateaus and smarter walkers; Local minimum), Chapter 13 (saddle point).

items.name: Convexity (strong convexity and subgradients)
items.formula: `f(λ × x + (1 − λ) × y) ≤ λ × f(x) + (1 − λ) × f(y)` for λ in [0, 1]; first-order test `f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x) · (y − x)`; second-order test: Hessian PSD everywhere; μ-strongly convex `f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x) · (y − x) + (μ ÷ 2) × ||y − x||^2`; subgradient g at x: `f(y) ≥ f(x) + g · (y − x)` for all y
items.meaning: A convex function is a bowl: the chord between any two points lies on or above the graph, every local minimum is global, and every tangent plane lies below the function. Strong convexity means the bowl curves up at least as fast as a parabola of curvature μ. Subgradients extend slopes to kinks such as |x| or ReLU at 0.
items.used_for: Linear and logistic regression, SVMs and linear probes have convex losses with guaranteed global solutions (classical-ml); deep networks are non-convex, so convex theory guides choices (learning-rate rules, optimizer derivations) without guaranteeing them; subgradients define what frameworks return at non-differentiable points. Book: Chapter 6 (Convex function definition).

items.name: Lipschitz continuity, L-smoothness and convergence rates
items.formula: Lipschitz `|f(x) − f(y)| ≤ K × ||x − y||`; L-smooth `||∇f(x) − ∇f(y)|| ≤ L × ||x − y||`, giving the descent lemma `f(x − (1 ÷ L) × ∇f(x)) ≤ f(x) − ||∇f(x)||^2 ÷ (2 × L)`; gradient descent with η = 1 ÷ L on convex f: `f(x_t) − f* ≤ L × ||x_0 − x*||^2 ÷ (2 × t)`; μ-strongly convex: error shrinks by a factor of about `(1 − μ ÷ L)` per step; SGD on convex problems: error about `1 ÷ sqrt(t)`
items.meaning: A Lipschitz bound K limits how fast a function can change; an L-smoothness bound limits how fast its slope can change (all Hessian eigenvalues at most L), which sets the largest safe step at about 1 ÷ L. f* is the minimum value and x* a minimizer; the ratio L ÷ μ is the condition number that sets how many steps are needed.
items.used_for: Theory behind learning-rate choices; spectral normalization enforces a Lipschitz bound on GAN discriminators and WGAN critics (generative-classical); certified-robustness bounds (rl-alignment); the modular-norm and Muon line of work picks per-layer step sizes from such bounds. Book: Only here.

items.name: Step-size stability on a quadratic (edge of stability)
items.formula: on `f(x) = (λ ÷ 2) × x^2`, gradient descent gives `x_(t+1) = (1 − η × λ) × x_t`, which converges only if `η < 2 ÷ λ`; in many dimensions, stable only if `η < 2 ÷ λ_max(H)`
items.meaning: Each step multiplies the distance to the bottom by (1 − η × λ); past η = 2 ÷ λ that factor drops below −1 and the iterates bounce outward and explode. The sharpest direction (largest Hessian eigenvalue λ_max) sets the limit. Appendix B's bowl (x − c)^2 has λ = 2, which gives its factor 1 − 2 × learning rate.
items.used_for: Explains learning-rate blow-ups and loss spikes; Cohen et al. (ICLR 2021) found that full-batch gradient descent on neural networks pushes the top Hessian eigenvalue up until it hovers just above 2 ÷ η (the 'edge of stability'); motivates warmup and sharpness-aware methods. Book: Chapter 6 (Choosing the step size; Worked: rolling down a parabola); Appendix B (Learning rate on a simple bowl).

items.name: Lagrange multipliers and KKT conditions
items.formula: minimize f(x) subject to g(x) = 0: `L(x, λ) = f(x) + λ × g(x)`, solve `∇f(x) + λ × ∇g(x) = 0` and `g(x) = 0`; with inequality constraints h_i(x) ≤ 0 (Karush–Kuhn–Tucker): `∇f + sum over j of λ_j × ∇g_j + sum over i of μ_i × ∇h_i = 0`, `μ_i ≥ 0`, `h_i(x) ≤ 0`, `μ_i × h_i(x) = 0`
items.meaning: At a constrained optimum the objective's gradient is balanced by the constraints' gradients. Each multiplier (λ or μ) is the 'price' of its constraint: how much the optimum would improve per unit of loosening. Complementary slackness (μ_i × h_i = 0) says a constraint that is not binding has zero price.
items.used_for: Deriving softmax as the maximum-entropy distribution with a fixed expected score; the closed-form optimal policy of KL-regularized RL that DPO builds on (rl-alignment); the SVM dual and its support vectors (classical-ml); constrained RLHF such as Safe RLHF's Lagrangian trade-off between helpfulness and harmlessness (Dai et al. 2023). Book: Only here.

items.name: Newton's method
items.formula: optimization `x_(t+1) = x_t − H(x_t)^-1 × ∇f(x_t)` (one variable: `x − f'(x) ÷ f''(x)`); root finding `x_(t+1) = x_t − f(x_t) ÷ f'(x_t)`; damped variant `x − (H + λ × I)^-1 × ∇f(x)`
items.meaning: Fit a parabola (the second-order Taylor model) at the current point and jump to its bottom. Near the answer it converges very fast (correct digits roughly double each step), but it needs the Hessian, which has N^2 entries for N parameters, so huge networks use approximations. Damping (adding λ × I) keeps steps safe far from the answer.
items.used_for: Iteratively reweighted least squares for logistic regression (classical-ml); Newton–Schulz iterations used by Muon are Newton-type iterations for a matrix function; second-order and approximate second-order optimizers (Shampoo, SOAP, K-FAC, Sophia) approximate H^-1; Levenberg–Marquardt fitting in robotics and vision. Book: Chapter 13 (curvature-based optimizers; Newton–Schulz iteration).

items.name: Quasi-Newton methods (BFGS and L-BFGS) and line search
items.formula: BFGS inverse-Hessian update `H_(k+1) = (I − ρ × s × y^T) × H_k × (I − ρ × y × s^T) + ρ × s × s^T` with `s = x_(k+1) − x_k`, `y = ∇f(x_(k+1)) − ∇f(x_k)`, `ρ = 1 ÷ (y^T × s)`; Armijo line search: accept step α if `f(x + α × d) ≤ f(x) + c × α × ∇f(x) · d`
items.meaning: Builds an approximation of the inverse Hessian from how the gradient changes between steps, instead of computing it. L-BFGS keeps only the last few (s, y) pairs, so memory stays small. A line search picks a step length α along direction d that lowers f by enough (c is a small constant such as 0.0001).
items.used_for: L-BFGS is scikit-learn's default solver for logistic regression (classical-ml); full-batch problems such as physics-informed networks, neural style transfer and fitting scaling-law curves (the Chinchilla paper fit its parametric loss with L-BFGS); rarely used for large stochastic training. Book: Only here.

items.name: Natural gradient
items.formula: `θ_(t+1) = θ_t − η × F^-1 × ∇L(θ_t)`, with F the Fisher information matrix
items.meaning: Steepest descent measured by how much the model's predictions change (KL divergence, whose local curvature is F) rather than by how much the raw parameter numbers change, so the step does not depend on how the model happens to be parameterized.
items.used_for: K-FAC approximates F^-1 with Kronecker factors (Martens & Grosse 2015); TRPO and natural policy gradient in reinforcement learning (rl-alignment); a common motivation for Adam-style and Shampoo-style preconditioning. Book: Only here.

items.name: Projected and proximal gradient methods (soft-thresholding)
items.formula: projected `x_(t+1) = Proj_C(x_t − η × ∇f(x_t))` with `Proj_C(z) = argmin over x in C of ||x − z||` (for an L-infinity ball of radius ε around x_0: clip each entry to [x_0 − ε, x_0 + ε]); proximal `x_(t+1) = prox_(η × λ × g)(x_t − η × ∇f(x_t))`, and for the L1 penalty `prox(z)_i = sign(z_i) × max(|z_i| − η × λ, 0)`
items.meaning: Projected descent takes a normal gradient step, then snaps back to the nearest allowed point in the set C. Proximal descent handles a smooth loss f with a gradient step and a non-smooth penalty g exactly; for L1 this soft-thresholding shrinks every entry toward zero and sets small ones exactly to zero, producing sparsity.
items.used_for: PGD adversarial attacks and adversarial training (Madry et al. 2018; robustness in rl-alignment); keeping weights nonnegative, unit-norm or on the probability simplex; lasso and elastic-net solvers apply soft-thresholding (scikit-learn's coordinate descent; classical-ml); sparse coding (ISTA). Book: Only here.

items.name: Steepest descent under a chosen norm
items.formula: `Δ = argmin over ||Δ|| ≤ η of (∇L · Δ)`; L2 norm: `Δ = −η × g ÷ ||g||_2`; L-infinity norm: `Δ = −η × sign(g)`; spectral norm on a weight matrix whose gradient is `G = U × Σ × V^T`: `Δ = −η × U × V^T`
items.meaning: What counts as 'most downhill' depends on how step size is measured. Measured by ordinary length, the best step follows the gradient; measured by the largest single entry, every parameter moves the same amount in the sign direction; measured by a matrix's largest stretch, every singular direction moves equally.
items.used_for: Bernstein & Newhouse (2024) showed that Adam, Shampoo and Prodigy, with their moving averages switched off, are each steepest descent under a particular norm; sign-based optimizers (signSGD, Lion) and Muon's orthogonalized updates are the L-infinity and spectral cases (deep-learning); the fast gradient-sign adversarial attack (FGSM). Book: Chapter 13 (Lion; Muon).

items.name: Mirror descent and exponentiated gradient (multiplicative weights)
items.formula: exponentiated gradient on probability weights `w_i ← w_i × exp(−η × g_i) ÷ sum over j of (w_j × exp(−η × g_j))`; general mirror descent `∇ψ(x_(t+1)) = ∇ψ(x_t) − η × ∇f(x_t)` for a mirror map ψ (negative entropy gives the exponentiated form)
items.meaning: Gradient descent carried out in a transformed space that suits the constraint. For probability weights each weight is multiplied by an exponential of its negative gradient and the weights are renormalized, so they stay positive and add to 1; ascent on a reward uses +η.
items.used_for: DoReMi tunes pretraining data-mixture weights with exponentiated-gradient ascent on per-domain excess loss (Xie et al. 2023); Hedge and multiplicative weights for online learning and solving games (game theory in rl-alignment); softmax policy updates in natural policy gradient. Book: Only here.

items.name: Binary integers and two's complement
items.formula: unsigned `value = sum over i of (b_i × 2^i)`; signed two's complement `value = −b_(n−1) × 2^(n−1) + sum over i < n − 1 of (b_i × 2^i)`; signed n-bit range `−2^(n−1)` to `2^(n−1) − 1` (INT8: −128 to 127; INT4: −8 to 7); bits needed to index K items `ceiling(log2(K))`
items.meaning: Computers write whole numbers in base 2, where bit b_i is worth 2^i. Two's complement gives the top bit a negative weight so the same adder circuits handle negative numbers.
items.used_for: INT8 and INT4 weights in quantized models (the scale-and-round step is in llm); token IDs (a 200,000-token vocabulary needs 18 bits, so IDs are stored as 32-bit integers); packing several 4-bit weights into one byte. Book: Chapter 2 (Counting in binary; Bytes and file sizes).

items.name: Floating-point value formula
items.formula: normal numbers `value = (−1)^s × (1 + m ÷ 2^M) × 2^(e − bias)` with `bias = 2^(E − 1) − 1`; subnormals (e = 0) `value = (−1)^s × (m ÷ 2^M) × 2^(1 − bias)`; formats as (E exponent bits, M mantissa bits): FP32 (8, 23), BF16 (8, 7), FP16 (5, 10), FP8 E4M3 (4, 3), FP8 E5M2 (5, 2), FP6 E2M3 and E3M2, FP4 E2M1 (2, 1)
items.meaning: s is the sign bit, e the stored exponent (E bits) and m the stored mantissa (M bits), the digits after an implicit leading 1. Exponent bits buy range; mantissa bits buy precision. Subnormal numbers fill the gap near zero. Several 8-bit and smaller formats drop or repurpose the infinity and NaN codes to gain range (FP4 E2M1 can only express 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 6 with a sign).
items.used_for: Every number in training and inference: FP32 master weights and accumulators, BF16 training, FP8 training and serving on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs (DeepSeek-V3 used E4M3 for all FP8 tensors), FP4 serving and the first FP4 pretraining runs. Book: Chapter 5 (Floating point; The precision ladder), Chapter 32 (How a computer stores a decimal number).

items.name: Range of a floating-point format (overflow and underflow)
items.formula: largest normal `(2 − 2^(−M)) × 2^(e_max − bias)` for IEEE-style formats (top exponent code reserved, so `e_max = 2^E − 2`); smallest normal `2^(1 − bias)`; smallest subnormal `2^(1 − bias − M)`; FP16 max `(2 − 2^−10) × 2^15 = 65,504`; BF16 and FP32 max ≈ 3.4 × 10^38; FP8 E4M3 max 448 (`1.75 × 2^8`, an exception because only one code is NaN); E5M2 max 57,344; FP4 E2M1 max 6
items.meaning: Exponent bits set how large and how small a format can go before overflowing to infinity or underflowing to zero. FP16 overflows past 65,504, which is why it needs loss scaling; BF16 copies FP32's 8 exponent bits, so it rarely overflows or underflows.
items.used_for: Choosing BF16 over FP16 for large-model training; the E4M3 (more precision) versus E5M2 (more range) trade-off in FP8; the need for per-block scale factors in FP8 and FP4, whose ranges are tiny. Book: Chapter 5 (The precision ladder table), Chapter 32 (FP16 and BF16 definitions).

items.name: Machine epsilon, unit roundoff and ULP
items.formula: `ε_mach = 2^(−M)` (the gap between 1 and the next representable number); unit roundoff `u = 2^(−M − 1)` (worst-case relative error of round-to-nearest); spacing near x `ulp(x) = 2^(floor(log2(|x|)) − M)`; FP32 ε ≈ 1.19 × 10^−7; FP16 ε ≈ 9.77 × 10^−4; BF16 ε = 2^−7 = 0.0078125
items.meaning: The relative precision of a format, roughly −log10(ε) significant decimal digits. The absolute gap between neighboring numbers (the ULP, unit in the last place) grows with the number's size, so a large running total cannot absorb small additions.
items.used_for: Explains why BF16 keeps only 2 to 3 significant digits and why optimizer states and accumulations stay in FP32; the small constant added inside Adam and normalization layers to avoid dividing by zero (also called epsilon, deep-learning) must be representable in the working format. Book: Chapter 5 (The precision ladder; Watch out on FP16 sums).

items.name: Rounding error model and catastrophic cancellation
items.formula: `fl(x) = x × (1 + δ)` with `|δ| ≤ u`; each operation `fl(a op b) = (a op b) × (1 + δ)`; relative error of a computed difference up to about `u × (|a| + |b|) ÷ |a − b|`
items.meaning: fl(x) is the stored (rounded) version of x. Every stored number and every arithmetic result is off by a tiny relative amount δ, at most the unit roundoff u. Subtracting two nearly equal numbers cancels their shared leading digits and leaves mostly rounding error (catastrophic cancellation).
items.used_for: Why variance is computed with stable algorithms (Welford's method, or subtracting the mean first) rather than E[x^2] − E[x]^2 in low precision; why softmax subtracts the maximum; why tiny logit differences vary across hardware (deep-learning, llm). Book: Chapter 5 (Why AI tolerates rough numbers).

items.name: Floating-point addition is not associative
items.formula: in floating point, in general `(a + b) + c ≠ a + (b + c)`; example in double precision: `(0.1 + 10^20) − 10^20 = 0` but `0.1 + (10^20 − 10^20) = 0.1`
items.meaning: Because every addition rounds, the order in which numbers are added changes the result slightly. Parallel hardware adds in different orders depending on how the work is split.
items.used_for: Thinking Machines Lab (Horace He and colleagues, September 2025) traced nondeterministic LLM outputs mainly to kernels that are not batch-invariant: the reduction order, and so the rounding, changes with batch size, which varies with server load; batch-invariant kernels restore reproducible results; also why results differ across GPU counts and parallelism layouts. Book: Chapter 18 (batch invariance).

items.name: Accumulation error in long sums (swamping, pairwise and Kahan summation)
items.formula: naive summation of n numbers: error up to about `(n − 1) × u × sum over i of |x_i|`; pairwise (tree) summation: about `log2(n) × u × sum over i of |x_i|`; Kahan compensated summation with running sum s and correction c: `y = x_i − c`, `t = s + y`, `c = (t − s) − y`, `s = t`
items.meaning: Adding many numbers one at a time lets rounding errors pile up, and once the running total is large, small additions are rounded away entirely (swamping: in FP16, adding 0.1 again and again gets stuck at 256). Adding in a tree, or carrying the lost low-order bits along (Kahan), keeps the error small.
items.used_for: Matrix-multiply hardware accumulates low-precision products at higher precision: DeepSeek-V3 found FP8 GEMM accumulation on H800 tensor cores keeps only about 14 bits, so it copies partial sums into FP32 every 128 elements (arXiv 2412.19437); FP32 gradient accumulation and all-reduce; Kahan summation and stochastic rounding for BF16-only weight updates (Zamirai et al., 'Revisiting BFloat16 Training', 2020). Book: Chapter 5 (Watch out: FP16 stuck at 256; Exercise 11).

items.name: Round-to-nearest-even and stochastic rounding
items.formula: round-to-nearest (ties to even): pick the closer of the neighbors `x_low ≤ x ≤ x_high`, breaking ties toward the one whose last bit is even; stochastic rounding `SR(x) = x_high` with probability `(x − x_low) ÷ (x_high − x_low)`, otherwise `x_low`, so `E[SR(x)] = x`
items.meaning: Ordinary rounding always moves the same input the same way, so tiny updates can be lost every single time. Stochastic rounding rounds up or down at random in proportion to closeness, so its error averages to zero and small updates survive on average.
items.used_for: NVIDIA's NVFP4 pretraining recipe (a 12-billion-parameter model on 10 trillion tokens) uses stochastic rounding for gradients and round-to-nearest-even for weights and activations (arXiv 2509.25149, 2025); low-precision training since Gupta et al. 2015; the OCP MX specification requires round-to-nearest-even for conversions to FP6 and FP4. Book: Only here.

items.name: Block-scaled (microscaling) formats: MXFP8, MXFP6, MXFP4 and NVFP4
items.formula: each value `v_i = X × P_i`, where a block of k elements P_1 to P_k shares one scale X; bits per value `= d + w ÷ k` (element bits d, scale bits w); OCP MX (2023): k = 32 and X is an E8M0 power of two `2^(stored − 127)`, so MXFP4 = 4 + 8 ÷ 32 = 4.25 bits; NVFP4: k = 16 with an FP8 E4M3 block scale plus one FP32 scale per tensor, about 4 + 8 ÷ 16 = 4.5 bits
items.meaning: Tiny formats such as FP4 hold only a handful of values, so each small block of numbers gets its own multiplier; one outlier then distorts only its own block. Smaller blocks and finer scales (NVFP4) follow the data more closely at a little extra storage. How the scales are chosen is part of quantization (llm).
items.used_for: OpenAI's gpt-oss stores its MoE weights in MXFP4 so gpt-oss-120b runs on a single 80 GB GPU (model card, August 2025); NVIDIA Blackwell and Rubin tensor cores run NVFP4 and MXFP4 natively; NVFP4 pretraining (NVIDIA 2025) and Nemotron 3 Super (March 2026); DeepSeek-V3's FP8 training used fine-grained scales per 1 × 128 activation tile and per 128 × 128 weight block. Book: Chapter 23 (Block scaling definition), Chapter 32 (rounding to FP4 and block scaling), Chapter 5 (At the frontier).

items.name: Loss scaling for FP16 training
items.formula: compute gradients of `S × L` instead of L, then use `g = ∇(S × L) ÷ S`; dynamic scaling: if any gradient is inf or NaN, skip the step and set `S ← S ÷ 2`, otherwise grow S periodically (for example double it after N good steps)
items.meaning: FP16's small range makes tiny gradients underflow to zero. Multiplying the loss by a large factor S lifts gradients into the representable range during backpropagation; dividing afterwards, in FP32, restores their true size.
items.used_for: Mixed-precision training in FP16 (Micikevicius et al. 2018; PyTorch's GradScaler); unnecessary with BF16, which has FP32's range, one reason BF16 became the default; the per-tensor and per-block scales of FP8 and FP4 training extend the same idea. Book: Chapter 32 (FP16 definition mentions loss scaling), Chapter 13 (Numbers on hardware).
